content: The duration of unconsciousness in the described case is not precisely known. However, it was noted that approximately 10 minutes later, the individual regained coherence, though they exhibited uncoordinated movements and experienced nausea. In one instance, 1 ppm of chloroform was detected in the exhaled breath of an individual. However, 12 days after exposure, no chloroform was detectable in their exhaled breath. Several studies have documented the concentration of chloroform in tissues following cases of suicide, homicide, or deaths occurring during or after surgical procedures. There are very few reports concerning industrial workers exposed to chloroform. Among the limited studies, those conducted by Challen et al. and Bomski et al. are notable for including measurements of exposure concentrations, descriptions of symptoms and diagnoses, and comparisons with control groups. In 1958, Challen et al. reported on a study involving a confectionery firm in England that manufactured medicinal lozenges. In 1950, workers began complaining about the chloroform vapor released during the production process. Symptoms included lassitude, flatulence, water brash (a term indicative of dyspepsia symptoms), dry mouth, thirst, depression, irritability, and frequent, painful urination described as scalding. A part-time work system was introduced to alleviate these complaints, but it proved ineffective. Eventually, the workers refused to continue working on that specific process. In 1954, a new team of operators was employed, and in 1955, an exhaust ventilation system was installed. Following this intervention, work proceeded without further interruptions. To confirm the effectiveness of the ventilation system, Challen and his colleagues were tasked with determining the concentrations of chloroform. Clinical investigations were also conducted, and efforts were made to simulate the original working conditions to compare chloroform concentrations before and after the implementation of remedial measures. The original conditions were recreated by closing doors and windows and turning off the ventilation system. Air sampling was conducted in the breathing zone of the operator during the ingredient mixing process over a 20-minute period, coinciding with the duration of the process. Air was drawn at a rate of 2 liters per minute through silica gel tubes. Additionally, a 6-liter grab sample was taken at a point in the operation where peak concentrations were expected. Thirty-minute air samples were also collected in the breathing zones of cutting room operators during two production periods for three different operations on the same day under current conditions, and during three periods on another day under simulated conditions. Challen et al. performed clinical investigations on three groups of workers. The first group, termed long service operators, consisted of eight employees who had refused to continue working in the lozenge department after experiencing the previously described symptoms. These workers had been exposed to chloroform vapor at probable concentrations ranging from 77 to 237 ppm and were observed staggering in the work area. After leaving the lozenge department, they reported nausea and stomach upset even after brief exposures to the smell of chloroform. The second group, termed short service operators, included nine employees who replaced the long service operators. Two of these nine employees did not report any adverse experiences from chloroform exposure. Among the remaining seven, five reported dryness of the mouth and throat at work, two experienced lassitude in the evening, one complained of lassitude and flatulence at work, and two others had experiences similar to those of the long service operators. These workers were exposed to chloroform concentrations ranging from 23 to 71 ppm. The third group, consisting of five employees working in other departments of the firm, served as controls and exhibited no symptoms. Tests of liver function (including thymol turbidity, thymol flocculation, direct van den Bergh, and serum bilirubin), clinical examinations, and urinary urobilinogen tests showed no significant differences among the three groups of workers. In 1967, Bomski et al. reported on liver injury caused by chloroform exposure among workers in a pharmaceutical factory in Poland. The study included 294 workers who used chloroform during production. Of these, 68 had been exposed to chloroform for 1–4 years and were still in contact with it, 39 had previous contact with chloroform, 23 had a history of viral hepatitis with jaundice 2–3 years earlier and were designated as post-icterus controls, and 165 worked in a germ-free area with no history of viral hepatitis. Various parameters were measured, including blood pressure, blood morphology, urinalysis, blood albumin, serum protein, thymol turbidity, zinc sulfate turbidity, the Takata-Ara sulfate test, urobilinogen, SGOT, and SGPT. A complete medical history was taken, and 60 individuals were hospitalized for determination of BSP clearance and urinary urobilinogen. Air samples from the production room were analyzed for chloroform concentrations using the Grabowicz method, with concentrations ranging from 2 to 205 ppm. No other concentration measurements or sampling frequency details were reported. The authors compared the frequency of viral hepatitis and jaundice among city inhabitants aged 18 and older with that of the 68 pharmaceutical workers exposed to chloroform. Sixty-seven percent of the chloroform-exposed workers had viral hepatitis, compared to 50.4% among the general population. The authors hypothesized that toxic liver changes resulting from chloroform exposure might promote viral infections in such cases. However, they did not provide data on the incidence of viral hepatitis among other plant workers, which could have clarified questions about sanitary practices and facilities in the plant. The majority of workers exposed to chloroform during the investigation period reported symptoms such as headache, nausea, belching, and loss of appetite. Among the 68 workers using chloroform, 10 cases of splenomegaly were identified, compared to none in the control group. The authors did not explain the splenomegaly but noted its absence in controls. The frequency of enlarged livers (17 out of 68) among workers exposed to chloroform exceeded that in other groups (5 out of 39 and 2 out of 23). Livers were considered enlarged if they extended at least 1 cm beyond the rib arch in the midclavicular line. The upper margin of the liver was not measured. In three of the 17 chloroform-exposed workers with liver enlargement, toxic hepatitis was diagnosed based on elevated serum enzyme activities and elevated serum gamma globulin levels.
